$comment: Exhibit wording applied to research/facility.json by scripts/build-facility.py. Number cards are keyed by research label, timeline entries by research date, and primer answers by explainer key. Sources, notes, physical values and published reference metadata remain in the research record. Authored display text uses plain sentences and straight quotes. Primer paragraphs are separated by a blank line. Brightness gains are design calculations, about 500 times overall and 100 to 1,000 times depending on X-ray energy.

Speed of the electrons.value: 99.9999996% of light speed, about 1.1 m/s slower than light
Speed of the electrons.explanation: At 6 GeV, an electron travels only about 1.1 m less than light in one second. Its energy is about 11,742 times its rest energy. This ratio is the Lorentz factor, γ = 6,000 MeV ÷ 0.511 MeV ≈ 11,742. The speed follows from 1 − v/c ≈ 1/(2γ²) = 3.6 × 10⁻⁹.

Laps per second.explanation: The lap rate is light speed divided by the ring's circumference, f₀ = c ÷ C = 299,792,458 m/s ÷ 1,103.61 m. The electrons move slowly enough below light speed that the difference is negligible here. The radio-frequency system runs at exactly 1,296 times the lap rate, about 352 MHz.
Laps per second.value: 271,647 laps around the 1.1 km ring each second

One lap.explanation: One lap takes 1 ÷ 271,647 of a second, or 3.68 microseconds. A microsecond is a millionth of a second. Each bunch of electrons sends a light pulse down each beamline once every 3.68 µs.

Distance per day.value: About 26 billion km per day, 173 times the Earth–Sun distance
Distance per day.explanation: An electron circulating for a whole day would travel 271,647 laps/s × 1.1036 km × 86,400 s ≈ 2.59 × 10¹⁰ km. That is about 173 times the Earth–Sun distance of 1.496 × 10⁸ km, enough for more than 80 round trips. In practice, each bunch is replaced about every 72 minutes.

Electrons in the ring.explanation: The beam current measures the charge passing a point each second. Each electron passes that point 271,647 times a second, so the stored charge is the current divided by the lap rate. At 0.2 A, this is 0.2 A ÷ 271,647 Hz = 736 nanocoulombs, or 4.6 × 10¹² electrons.

Electrons in one bunch.value: About 21 billion in 216-bunch mode, up to about 65 billion in 48-bunch timing mode
Electrons in one bunch.explanation: In 216-bunch mode, each bunch carries 736 nC ÷ 216 = 3.4 nC, or 2.1 × 10¹⁰ electrons. In 48-bunch timing mode, each carries about 10 to 11 nC, or 6.2 to 6.7 × 10¹⁰ electrons. The injector limits timing-mode current to 130 to 140 mA. The 200 mA design would require 15.3 nC, or 9.6 × 10¹⁰ electrons, per bunch.

Bunch spacing.value: 17 ns in 216-bunch mode, 77 ns in timing mode
Bunch spacing.explanation: The radio-frequency field creates 1,296 stable slots, called buckets, spaced 2.84 ns apart. Filling every sixth bucket gives 216 bunches at 17 ns intervals. This assumes even spacing; the exact fill pattern is not published. Filling every 27th bucket gives 48 bunches at 76.7 ns intervals. A nanosecond is a billionth of a second.

Ring size.value: 1,103.6 m around, about 350 m across, with 40 sectors
Ring size.explanation: The ring has 40 identical sectors, each 27.59 m long, for a circumference of 1,103.61 m. Rounded to 27.6 m per sector, this is about 1.1 km. A circle with that circumference would be about 351 m across. The actual ring consists of curved arcs joined by straight sections.

A slightly smaller ring.explanation: The straight sections containing the undulators stayed in place, so their beamlines needed re-surveying and fine alignment. Fitting new arcs between these fixed points shortened the ring from 1,103.99 m to 1,103.61 m. Each bending-magnet source moved about 1.8 m upstream and 42 mm toward the ring's centre, requiring beamline realignment. The shorter path also raised the radio frequency by about 342 parts per million.
A slightly smaller ring.value: 38 cm shorter than the old ring

Magnets.explanation: Each sector contains 33 magnets, and one extra corrector sits near injection. The total is 33 × 40 + 1 = 1,321, of 15 main types. Each sector has 7 forward bending magnets and 6 reverse bends, which are quadrupoles mounted off-centre to add a small backward bend. It also has 10 further quadrupoles to focus the beam, 6 sextupoles to correct focusing across electron energies, and 4 fast steering correctors. The old ring had 80 dipoles, 400 quadrupoles, 280 sextupoles, 317 correctors and 20 skew quadrupoles.
Magnets.value: 1,321 electromagnets, compared with 1,097 before the upgrade

Bending magnets per sector.explanation: Each sector turns the beam through a net 9°, or 360° ÷ 40. Seven forward bends spread this turn over more magnets, reducing the growth of the electron beam. Six small reverse bends change how electrons of different energies spread through the arc. They reduced the design emittance, the beam size multiplied by its angular spread, from 67 to 42 pm·rad.
Bending magnets per sector.value: 7 forward and 6 reverse bends, replacing 2 forward bends

Total bending.value: About 435° of bending per lap, with a net turn of 360°
Total bending.explanation: Some magnets bend the beam backward, so the forward bends must turn it through more than 360°. The forward turns total +397.8° and the backward turns −37.7°. Together they give about 435° of bending, while the net turn closes the ring at 360°.

Magnet strength.value: Quadrupole gradients of about 80 to 100 T/m, compared with about 20 T/m before
Magnet strength.explanation: A quadrupole's gradient measures how quickly its magnetic field increases away from the beam axis. A larger gradient provides stronger focusing. The new gradients are about 4 to 5 times the old value. They require bores about 26 mm across and pole tips made from vanadium permendur, a cobalt–iron alloy that supports stronger fields than ordinary magnet iron.

Pre-built modules.value: 200 modules, each up to about 6.5 m long and 27 tonnes
Pre-built modules.explanation: The magnets were mounted and aligned on supports in an off-site workspace before the shutdown. Each module was carried into the tunnel on a Traksporter, placed within 25 mm of its final position, aligned to 1 mm and grouted to the floor. Each sector has five modules, named DLM-A, QMQ-A, FODO, QMQ-B and DLM-B. The central FODO module is the heaviest, about 27 tonnes over 6.3 m. The two DLM modules are the longest, about 6.5 m.

Installation pace.explanation: All 200 magnet modules were installed between 12 July and 20 December 2023. Over those 162 days, installation averaged about 1.2 modules per calendar day.

Alignment.value: 15 µm rms within each module, against a 30 µm specification
Alignment.explanation: Within each module, magnets share a support and are aligned to 15 µm rms. Root-mean-square, or rms, measures the typical deviation from alignment. The specification was 30 µm. After installation, alignment between modules measured 50 µm horizontally and 35 µm vertically rms, within the ±100 µm specification around the 1.1 km ring.

Vibration budget.explanation: The electron beam must stay steady to within 10% of its size. A moving quadrupole deflects the beam passing through it, so vibration between 1 and 100 cycles per second is limited to 10 nm rms. Root-mean-square, or rms, measures the typical vibration amplitude.
Vibration budget.value: 10 nm rms for quadrupole vibration at 1 to 100 Hz

Beam size at an undulator.value: About 12 × 8 µm rms in round-beam user mode, compared with 275 × 10 µm before
Beam size at an undulator.explanation: The zero-current model sizes are 12.3 × 8.3 µm rms in round-beam mode, or about 29 × 19 µm full width at half maximum. Root-mean-square, or rms, describes the width of the electron distribution. The old beam was 275 × 10 µm rms, roughly half a millimetre wide at half maximum. The flat-mode sizes are 14.5 × 3.1 µm rms, about 14 × 3 µm rounded. The cross-sectional area is about 27 to 62 times smaller than before, depending on mode.

Emittance.value: About 42 pm·rad natural emittance, compared with 3,100 pm·rad before; 28 to 44 pm·rad measured
Emittance.explanation: Emittance is beam size multiplied by angular spread, in picometre-radians. The natural, or model, value is 41.5 pm·rad, giving 3,100 ÷ 41.5 ≈ 75 times less than before. APS describes this as "almost a factor of 100". Measurements depend on coupling, the sharing of emittance between the two planes. They give 44 pm·rad horizontally in flat mode, or 28 horizontally and 31 vertically in round mode. The old vertical value was 40 pm·rad, so most of the round-mode improvement is horizontal.

Brightness.value: About 500 times brighter; 100 to 1,000 times depending on X-ray energy
Brightness.explanation: Brightness measures photon output per source area, angular spread and narrow energy band. A smaller, more parallel source and twice the current give a design gain of ×540 at 20 keV for an undulator optimized for that energy. Other design estimates are roughly ×200 at 10 keV and ×600 to ×800 at 50 to 100 keV. Coherent flux gains are about ×160 at 10 keV and ×600 at 20 keV. These are calculations, not measured brightness gains.

Vacuum chamber.value: 22 mm wide, compared with a 42 × 85 mm chamber before; undulator chambers are 6.3 mm tall
Vacuum chamber.explanation: The 22 mm vacuum pipe leaves space for magnet poles close to the beam, supporting stronger focusing. Inside insertion devices, or undulators, the chamber is flattened to 6.3 mm tall with 0.6 mm walls. Most devices have an 8.5 mm design minimum magnet gap.

Power radiated by the beam.value: About 0.59 MW from bending magnets, up to about 0.9 MW with all undulators closed
Power radiated by the beam.explanation: Each electron loses about 2.94 MeV as radiation in the bending magnets per lap in the as-built model; the 2019 design gave 2.87 MeV. At 0.2 A, this is 587 kW. Closing every undulator gap raises the loss to 4.47 MeV per lap, or 894 kW. Twelve radio-frequency cavities replace the lost energy on every lap.

Energy stored in the beam.explanation: Stored energy is charge multiplied by energy per unit charge, 736 nC × 6 GV = 4.42 kJ. For comparison, a 1,000 kg car moving at 2.97 m/s has the same kinetic energy, from ½mv², or about 3 m/s rounded. The beam concentrates this energy in a small cross-section. Before a full-beam dump, a fan-out kicker magnet spreads the bunches across the dump surface.

Swap-out.value: One depleted bunch is replaced about every 20 seconds
Swap-out.explanation: The stable region in the new ring is too small to add electrons to stored bunches, so whole bunches are replaced during experiments. Kicker pulses about 11 ns long select one bunch without hitting neighbours 17 ns away. Each of the 216 bunches is renewed about every 72 minutes, from 216 × 20 s. With a beam lifetime of about 2 hours, it has then lost about 45% of its charge. A fresh bunch carries 5.4 to 6.1 nC, about 35 billion electrons.

Superconducting harmonic cavity.value: Niobium at 2.1 K, or −271 °C; bunches lengthen by a factor of 2 to 4
Superconducting harmonic cavity.explanation: The passing bunches excite the cavity at 1.4 GHz, four times the main radio frequency. The cavity has no external power source. Its electric field lengthens the bunches, reducing electron collisions that remove particles from the beam. In operation this roughly doubles the beam lifetime; the design expected a factor of four.

Beam position monitors.explanation: Fourteen pickups in each of 40 sectors measure the beam position so its orbit can be corrected. As of 2025, software corrections run up to 50 times per second. Fast orbit feedback with a 1 kHz bandwidth was removed from the project's scope and is being completed by the operating facility.
Beam position monitors.value: 560 pickups measure the beam position around the ring

Power supplies.explanation: There are 1,002 unipolar supplies, with current in one direction, and 921 slow bipolar supplies, with current in either direction. Another 322 are fast supplies. Two supplies each drive a string of bending magnets in series, one for all M1 bends and one for all M2 bends.

Dark time.value: 352 days from 24 April 2023 shutdown to 10 April 2024 commissioning; first beamline X-rays after 420 days
Dark time.explanation: The old ring was removed in 60 days. Crews then installed 200 magnet modules and assembled, tested and vacuum-baked the new ring. The first stored beam came 10 days into commissioning. X-rays first reached beamline 27-ID on 17 June 2024.

Old ring removed.value: About 1,900 tons planned for disposal or recycling, including about 200 girders of 6.8 to 11.3 tons each
Old ring removed.explanation: Some old magnets were retained for reuse. Jefferson Lab and Brookhaven National Laboratory received magnets for the Electron-Ion Collider project.

Cost.explanation: The US Department of Energy fixed the project cost in December 2018 when it approved the performance baseline, Critical Decision 2. Argonne reports that the upgrade was delivered within that budget.

Users.explanation: The APS and partner institutions operate beamlines for materials science, chemistry, biology, geoscience and engineering. In its first year of user operation, the upgraded ring delivered beam for 96.5% of scheduled hours.
Users.value: More than 5,500 scientists annually; 72 beamlines; 5,000 user hours per year

Undulator precision.value: 0.5 µm gap resolution, repeatability better than 3 µm; about 1 eV energy control at a 1 keV/s scan rate
Undulator precision.explanation: An undulator's magnet gap sets its X-ray energy. Reproducing the gap within micrometres keeps that energy accurate to about one electron-volt, even during scans at 1 keV per second.

Beam height.explanation: The 2019 Final Design Report specifies this height in its straight-section drawings. It places the electron beam roughly at adult chest height.

1995-03-18.event: Electrons make their first turn around the original APS storage ring. On 25 March, the radio-frequency system first captures them in stable bunches.

2010-04-27.event: The US Department of Energy approves the need for an APS upgrade. This is Critical Decision 0, or CD-0, the first formal approval for a major DOE project.

2014-03.event: A July 2013 report by DOE's Basic Energy Sciences Advisory Committee recommends multi-bend-achromat rings. Around 2014, APS physicist Michael Borland outlines an initial APS design in technical note LS-337. The date is approximate.

2016-02-04.event: DOE approves the multi-bend-achromat design and the project's cost range under a revised Critical Decision 1, or CD-1.

2016-06-09.event: DOE's Basic Energy Sciences Advisory Committee describes the upgrade as "absolutely central" and "ready to initiate construction".

2016-10-06.event: DOE approves advance purchases of components with long manufacturing times. This is the CD-3B procurement approval.

2018-12-13.event: DOE approves the project's scope, schedule and $815 million budget. This CD-2 approval establishes the performance baseline.

2019-05.event: The project publishes the Final Design Report, APSU-2.01-RPT-003, detailing the new ring and beamlines.

2019-07-25.event: DOE approves construction of the $815 million upgrade under CD-3.

2021-05.event: The project has incurred half its planned cost. COVID-19 delays have moved expected first beam back ten months to mid-2024.

2023-04-24.event: The original APS storage ring shuts down permanently. Experiments begin a planned period of about a year without X-rays.

2023-06-23.event: Removal of the old storage ring is complete, 60 days after shutdown.

2023-07-12.event: The first of 200 pre-assembled magnet modules is installed in the tunnel.

2023-09.event: The linear accelerator restarts. The particle accumulator ring follows in October 2023 and the booster synchrotron in February 2024.

2023-10-27.event: The first vacuum bake-out begins. Heating the chambers under vacuum removes gas from their walls.

2023-12-20.event: The last of 200 magnet modules is installed, 162 days after the first.

2024-02-15.event: The last component is installed, completing storage-ring assembly.

2024-03-24.event: Testing and vacuum bake-out of the new ring are complete.

2024-03-25/28.event: An Accelerator Readiness Review checks that the new accelerator can operate safely.

2024-04-10.event: DOE authorizes commissioning. Operators can begin circulating beam and tuning the new ring.

2024-04-13.event: Electrons make their first turns around the new ring.

2024-04-20.event: The ring stores its first beam at 0.15 mA. Electrons continue circulating rather than being lost after a few turns.

2024-04-29.event: APS-U performs the world's first multi-bunch swap-out injection. With 12 bunches stored, the weakest is replaced every 30 seconds.

2024-05-02.event: The septum magnet fails when its copper current bar ruptures after about a million pulses. This pulsed magnet directs incoming electrons into the ring. Beam operation resumes ten days later.

2024-05-12.event: The ring stores 10 mA across many bunches. From 17 May, radiation from the beam removes gas from chamber walls in a process called vacuum conditioning.

2024-05-17.event: Stored current reaches 25 mA, enough for beamline commissioning. The milestone is announced the next day.

2024-06-02.event: The spare septum magnet develops a vacuum leak. The repaired original is reinstalled.

2024-06-17.event: At 50 mA, X-rays first reach scientific beamline 27-ID for resonant inelastic X-ray scattering. The period dedicated to machine commissioning ends.

2024-07-17.event: The upgraded APS is formally dedicated.

2024-08.event: Measurements at 3-ID-B and 29-ID confirm the lowest emittance of any storage-ring light source at the time. Emittance, beam size multiplied by angular spread, is 45 pm·rad horizontally in flat mode and 28 pm·rad horizontally in round mode. The results are announced on 23 August.

2024-09.event: Round-the-clock user experiments begin at 100 mA, with a 162-bunch mode and a 48-bunch timing mode.

2024-10-08.event: The superconducting bunch-lengthening cavity is first used during user runs at 0.5 MV. By 2025 it operates at 1.1 MV with 200 mA stored.

2025-01-27.event: Beam returns after the winter shutdown, and the first 2025 user run begins at 180 mA. The first half uses standard multi-bunch mode; the second uses timing mode. There are 27 beamlines accepting users and 43 in commissioning.

2025-02-04.event: The ring reaches its 200 mA design current, twice the old current, and uses it for user operation.

2025-04.event: Horizontal emittance is measured at about 33 pm·rad with 200 mA stored. The operating conditions are not stated.

2025-07.event: HEXM at 20-ID measures its first sample. CHEX at 28-ID receives first light in all four branches, and sector 34 also receives first light.

2025-08.event: Argonne holds a director's review of project delivery before DOE's CD-4 completion review.

2025-09 (late).event: DOE reviewers unanimously recommend project completion under Critical Decision 4, or CD-4, followed by close-out.

2025-10.event: PtychoProbe at 33-ID and ATOMIC at 34-ID enter commissioning. All feature beamlines have reached commissioning or user operation, and 51 beamlines are accepting users.

2025-10-08.event: After its first year of user operation, the new ring has delivered beam for 96.5% of scheduled hours. It runs at 200 mA in 216-bunch mode and 140 mA in 48-bunch timing mode. The beam is round and fully coupled, with a lifetime of 2 to 4 hours.

2025-11.event: The PtychoProbe instrument is installed at 33-ID, the last feature beamline built by the project.

2026-01-29.event: The project reports that all planned work has been delivered. DOE is reviewing formal completion, and the first 2026 user run is scheduled for 2 February.

2026-02-05.event: DOE announces final approval of the APS Upgrade. The $815 million project delivered 9 new beamlines and 15 enhancements.

2026-06-10.event: The APS begins replacing the klystron vacuum-tube amplifiers that power its radio-frequency cavities with solid-state amplifiers. Four are being installed for one sector's four cavities. Storage-ring conversion is expected by 2028, followed by the booster.

2026-09-22.event: As of September 2026, the eight superconducting undulators planned for sectors 1, 11, 20 and 28 are delayed and not installed. Permanent-magnet devices remain in use there and at sector 6, where the 2019 design also specified a superconducting device.

explainers.whatIsSynchrotron:
A synchrotron light source circulates electrons to produce light. At the APS, a linear accelerator, or linac, starts the electrons. A small accumulator ring gathers them into bunches, and a booster ring accelerates them to 6 billion electron-volts, or 6 GeV. At this energy they move at 99.9999996% of light speed. They circulate in a 1.1 km storage ring, where magnets bend their paths. The electrons emit radiation in a narrow forward cone as they bend.

The radiation spans infrared through hard X-rays. The APS uses the X-rays to study materials and biological samples. Undulators, rows of alternating magnets in 35 of the 40 straight sections, produce the brightest beams. Beamlines carry them to experiment stations. Twelve radio-frequency cavities replace the 2.9 to 4.5 MeV each electron loses per lap, depending on how many undulator gaps are closed. Replacing one depleted bunch about every 20 seconds keeps the current steady.
explainers.whatIsUndulator:
An undulator has two rows of magnets with alternating north and south poles. Most APS devices are about 2.1 to 2.4 m long, with a magnetic pattern repeating every 1.35 to 3.3 cm. This repeat distance is the period. Electrons deflect from side to side about 60 to 175 times per pass. Radiation from these deflections reinforces at particular wavelengths, producing a narrow beam at a fundamental energy and its harmonics. The harmonics are higher-energy multiples of the fundamental. Opening or closing the magnet gap changes the field and tunes the X-ray energy. Most devices have an 8.5 mm design minimum gap, controlled with half-micrometre resolution. Sector 29 has a special electromagnetic device with a 12.5 cm period.

Superconducting undulators use wire coils cooled to −269 °C to produce stronger fields for high-energy X-rays. Eight are planned for APS-U. Sectors 1 and 20 each have an in-line pair with 16.5 mm periods and 1.9 m lengths. Sector 11 has two devices angled apart to feed independent beamlines, with 16.5 mm periods and 1.5 m lengths. Sector 28 has an angled pair with 18.5 mm periods and 1.2 to 1.3 m lengths. Manufacturing delays mean none was installed as of September 2026. Permanent-magnet devices are in use instead.
explainers.whatIsMBA:
Each of the APS ring's 40 sectors turns the electron beam through a net 9°. The old ring used two main bends per sector. Emitting photons changes the electrons' energies randomly, which contributes to beam spreading. A multi-bend achromat, or MBA, distributes the turn among more bends and uses focusing magnets between them. Theory predicts that emittance, beam size multiplied by angular spread, decreases roughly as the cube of the number of bends per sector. Changing from two to seven bends alone gives about a 40-fold reduction.

APS-U uses a hybrid seven-bend achromat based on the ESRF-EBS design at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The bending-magnet field decreases along each magnet. Six off-centre quadrupoles per sector add small reverse bends to control how electrons of different energies spread through the arc. These reduced the design emittance from about 67 to 42 picometre-radians, or pm·rad. With electron energy also reduced from 7 to 6 GeV, the change from the old ring is about 3,100 to 42 pm·rad. An achromat returns electrons with slightly different energies to the same path at the sector exit.
explainers.whyEmittanceMatters:
Emittance measures electron-beam size multiplied by angular spread. X-rays inherit both the source size and the spread of electron directions. A small, nearly parallel source can be focused to nanometre spots and remains narrow on the path to distant experiments. A smaller electron beam also increases the fraction of X-rays usable for coherent measurements.

APS-U reduced the horizontal emittance about 75-fold, from 3,100 to 42 pm·rad. Horizontal × vertical rms source sizes changed from about 275 × 10 µm to about 12 × 8 µm in round-beam user mode, or about 14 × 3 µm in flat mode. Root-mean-square, or rms, describes the electron distribution's width. This smaller source and twice the current give about 500 times greater brightness by design, with gains of 100 to 1,000 times depending on X-ray energy. The gain is greatest at high energies, where the old source was furthest from the diffraction limit. Near this limit, about wavelength divided by 4π in emittance, reducing the electron beam adds little.
explainers.whatIsCoherence:
Coherent light maintains a consistent relationship between its wave phases, so overlapping waves produce stable interference patterns. A laser is highly coherent; light from a bulb is much less so. For a fully coherent X-ray source, size multiplied by angular spread must be below about wavelength divided by 4π. This is roughly 10 pm·rad at 10 keV.

A larger source is partly coherent, so only a fraction of its photons is usable for coherent experiments. At 10 keV this was well below 0.1% at the old APS and is a few percent at APS-U. Better undulators and twice the current increase coherent flux further. Design gains are more than 100-fold, about 160 times at 10 keV and 600 times at 20 keV. Ptychography and coherent diffraction imaging reconstruct images from interference patterns called speckle. Their resolution depends on how far the scattered signal can be recorded. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, or XPCS, measures motion from changes in speckle, including motion of nanoparticles, polymer chains and magnetic domains.
explainers.whatIsSwapOut:
The old APS added electrons to stored bunches every minute or two to maintain current. This top-up injection needed a large stable region around the stored beam. Stronger focusing leaves a stable region only about ±1.5 mm at the new injection point. APS-U therefore replaces whole depleted bunches with fresh ones from the booster.

A few hundred turns before a swap, a small decoherence kick spreads the outgoing bunch to prevent damage at the dump. Three fast kicker magnets then direct it into a shielded dump and place a fresh bunch in the same slot. Their pulses last about 11 ns, short enough to miss neighbouring bunches 17 ns away. In 2025 operation, one swap occurred about every 20 seconds, renewing each of 216 bunches roughly every 72 minutes. APS-U is the first storage-ring light source to operate this way.
explainers.whatIsBunchLengthening:
Electrons in dense bunches occasionally scatter off one another and leave the stored beam. This loss process is Touschek scattering. A superconducting niobium harmonic cavity lengthens the bunches to reduce their density without widening the beam. It operates at 2.1 K, or −271 °C. The passing bunches excite a field at four times the main radio frequency, lengthening them by a factor of 2 to 4.

At 1.1 MV and 200 mA, the cavity roughly doubles the beam lifetime in operation. The design expected about a fourfold increase. Longer bunches produce longer X-ray pulses. The design bunch lengths are about 88 to 104 ps rms, depending on fill pattern. A picosecond is a trillionth of a second; rms describes the width of the bunch distribution.
explainers.whyLowerEnergy:
APS-U reduced electron energy from 7 to 6 billion electron-volts, or GeV. For a fixed lattice, emittance grows with energy squared, so this reduction alone gives about 36% more brightness. Lower energy also allows weaker magnets for the same focusing. Radiation loss per lap scales with energy to the fourth power. Reducing that loss makes a 200 mA current, twice the old value, possible within the radio-frequency power capacity.

The tradeoff is lower photon energy, about 27% less for each undulator harmonic. Shorter-period undulators and higher harmonics compensate for this. Lower-energy bunches are also more sensitive to instabilities caused by their own electromagnetic fields and to collisions between their electrons.
explainers.whyRoundBeams:
APS-U usually shares emittance about equally between the horizontal and vertical planes. This is full coupling. Each plane measures about 28 to 31 pm·rad, producing a nearly round beam. Spreading electrons vertically lowers bunch density and reduces losses from Touschek scattering, collisions that remove electrons from the beam. The design used round beams as the default operating mode.

Flat mode has low coupling and emittances of about 40 × 4 pm·rad. Its smaller vertical source gives higher brightness but a shorter lifetime. It is workable with many bunches in the ring. In round mode, the measured vertical emittance of about 31 pm·rad is close to the old ring's 40 pm·rad. Most of the round-mode improvement is therefore horizontal.
